summary: The Lord gathers all nations in the valley of Josaphat to plead with them — they have scattered his people, divided his land, sold boys and girls for wine. Tyre, Sidon, and the coasts of the Greeks are named for the slave trade. Then the summons to war: 'Beat your ploughshares into swords, and your sickles into spears' — the harvest of judgment, the sun and moon darkened, the Lord roaring from Zion. And after judgment: the mountains dripping sweet wine, a fountain from the house of the Lord, and 'the Lord shall dwell in Sion.'
whyItMatters: This is the chapter where Joel's locust plague becomes the template for 'the day of the Lord' — judgment on the nations that trafficked God's people. Its ploughshare-sword reversal is one of prophecy's boldest images, and its ending fountain feeds Ezekiel's river and, downstream, the water of life in Revelation.

keyVerses.text: I will also gather all the Gentiles, and bring them down to the valley of Josaphat, and will plead with them there for my people and my heritage Israel, who have been dispersed among the Gentiles; and these Gentiles have divided my land.
keyVerses.why: Josaphat means 'the Lord judges' — the valley is less a map location than a courtroom where history's trafficking of God's people comes to trial.

keyVerses.text: Beat your ploughshares into swords, and your sickles into spears: let the weak say, I am strong.
keyVerses.why: The deliberate reversal of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3 — where God beats swords into ploughshares for peace, here the instruments of farming become weapons, because the nations chose war first.

keyVerses.text: Noises have resounded in the valley of judgment: for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of judgment.
keyVerses.why: The chapter names its own theme: 'the day of the Lord' — the phrase Joel made famous — arriving as harvest.

keyVerses.text: And it shall come to pass in that day that the mountains shall drop sweet wine, and the hills shall flow with milk, and all the fountains of Juda shall flow with water, and a fountain shall go forth of the house of the Lord, and water the valley of flags.
keyVerses.why: After judgment, abundance — the fountain from the temple that Ezekiel sees becoming a river, and that Revelation places in the New Jerusalem.

themes: Restoration and the river of God

questions.question: Why does my Bible have only three chapters of Joel?
questions.answer: Numbering, not content. The Hebrew text divides Joel differently: what the Septuagint (and this arrangement) calls chapter 4 is Hebrew Joel 3, and Hebrew 2:28-32 (Peter's Pentecost quotation) is Greek chapter 3. Same words, different chapter lines — which is why this chapter's opening 'in those days' continues the Spirit-outpouring promise.

questions.question: What is the valley of Josaphat?
questions.answer: Josaphat (Jehoshaphat) means 'the Lord judges.' No such valley is named on ancient maps of Judah — it is a symbolic site, the place where God pleads his people's case against the nations. Later tradition located it in the Kidron valley east of Jerusalem, and Joel's picture fed centuries of expectation about a last judgment.

questions.question: Why reverse 'swords into ploughshares'?
questions.answer: Isaiah and Micah promise a future where God beats swords into ploughshares — peace after war. Joel shows the other half: for nations that refused peace and trafficked people, the ploughshares go back into swords. The two images are one prophecy's two edges — peace for the obedient, war for the predators.

questions.question: Who are 'the children of the Greeks'?
questions.answer: The Ionian Greeks of Asia Minor — partners in the Phoenician slave trade that moved captives through Tyre and Sidon's markets. The charge is specific: 'ye have sold the children of Juda... that ye might expel them from their coasts' (4:6). Human trafficking is the named crime the judgment answers.

questions.question: How does this chapter connect to the rest of the Bible?
questions.answer: Downstream everywhere: Jesus locates the judgment of the nations in the valley of decision language (Matthew 25's sheep and goats echo the gathering); Revelation 14's harvest and 22's river of life draw on the sickle and the fountain; and Acts 2 quotes the chapter just before this one. Joel 4 is where the Bible's judgment-and-river imagery meets.
